Why is Gaza drowning? Images of floods engulfing Gaza have gone viral. Most coverage focuses on the humanitarian catastrophe. Few explain what caused it. Since October 2023, Israeli forces have destroyed nearly all of Gaza’s infrastructure. Up to 68 million tons of rubble now blanket the Strip. Homes, schools, hospitals, and basic services have been flattened, with at least 90 percent of the territory destroyed. Now, as winter sets in, the first rains are making what is left unlivable. At least five people have been killed after sand embankments collapsed in the downpour. None of this is new. The Israeli plan to make Gaza unlivable has been unfolding for years. In 2012, the UN warned that Gaza could be unlivable by 2020 because of repeated Israeli assaults, a crippling blockade, the collapse of its aquifer, energy shortages, and mass unemployment. Despite the so-called ceasefire, our reporter in Gaza describes a situation that is impossible to endure: no shelter, no aid, and a ban on rebuilding. Conditions are getting worse by the day.” @specter_affairs

This year’s olive harvest has been the most violent in recent memory, with settler attacks on Palestinian farmers reaching a new high. But for Masafer Yatta, this is only the latest escalation in a decades-long campaign by the Israeli state to expel Palestinians from their land by any means necessary. Working in coordination with the army and police, nearby settlers wage a ceaseless battle against the Palestinians living in this area. Professor Ilan Pappé describes what has been happening to Masafer Yatta since the 1970’s as “incremental colonization, ethnic cleansing, and oppression,” and to be here is to see it firsthand. But the people of Masafer Yatta have earned a reputation for themselves for their resistance to state and settler terror. They simply refuse to leave, and the Israelis simply won’t stop trying to force them to. The Nakba never ended. We’re just watching its latest act.

Naji Abu Awad, a Palestinian American based in Texas, returned to his hometown of Turmus’ayya in the occupied West Bank to take back his family home after Israeli soldiers broke in and occupied it for more than two weeks, turning it into a military outpost. When Naji arrived, Israeli soldiers confronted him with guns and smoke grenades. Imagine being unable to leave your home because Israeli soldiers or settlers might use your absence to take it from you. For Palestinians across the occupied West Bank, that fear is part of daily life. Home theft, settler attacks, and forced displacement are not isolated incidents. They are part of a system designed to make Palestinian life increasingly impossible while expanding Israeli control over Palestinian land.

videos.caption: 🇵🇸 After enduring genocide, displaced Palestinians in Gaza are now facing torrential rain and flooding in the camps where they sought shelter. In its October 26 report, the UN's independent commission of inquiry said the genocide was ongoing. On November 7, Gaza's Civil Defence reported around 1,500 calls for help in just 10 hours. The Hamas-run government media office estimated that around 70,000 tents flooded in 12 hours. Before the storm, the UN had already warned of shortages of tents, tarps and blankets. Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter supplies and funding shortfalls had hampered preparations for winter. Families need waterproof shelters, dry blankets and pumps to drain the flooded camps. Those forced out of their tents need somewhere safe to sleep tonight. #Gaza #freepalestine #freepalestine🇵🇸❤️ #Palestine #palestine🇵🇸
